objectives: Write the six-factor formula + interpret each factor.
Apply the diffusion equation to simple geometries.

slides.title: k-effective + the six-factor formula
slides.body:
**k-effective** (k_eff) = ratio of neutrons in one generation to the previous. Three regimes:
• k < 1: subcritical (chain dies out)
• k = 1: critical (steady state)
• k > 1: supercritical (chain grows)

For an infinite reactor (no leakage): **k_∞ = η · f · p · ε** (four-factor formula).
With leakage in finite reactor: **k_eff = k_∞ · P_NL** where P_NL is non-leakage probability.

Six-factor: k_eff = η · f · p · ε · P_NL,fast · P_NL,thermal.

Meanings:
• **η** (reproduction): neutrons emitted per thermal neutron absorbed in fuel. η = ν · σ_f / σ_a. For U-235: ~2.07. For Pu-239: ~2.11.
• **f** (thermal utilization): fraction of thermal neutron absorption that occurs in fuel (vs moderator, structure, coolant). Typical PWR: ~0.7.
• **p** (resonance escape): probability that a fast neutron slows down through U-238 resonances without being captured. ~0.75-0.80.
• **ε** (fast fission factor): bonus fission from fast neutrons in U-238 before they thermalize. ~1.03.
• **P_NL**: depends on reactor size + reflector. Large core: P_NL ≈ 0.95.

For a typical PWR: 2.07 × 0.7 × 0.78 × 1.03 × 0.95 ≈ 1.10 — needs poison (boron, control rods) to bring k_eff to 1.0. As fuel depletes + fission products build up, k_∞ drops; operators withdraw poison to maintain criticality.

slides.title: Neutron diffusion equation
slides.body:
For a homogeneous medium, neutron flux φ (n cm⁻² s⁻¹) satisfies the **diffusion equation**:

  D ∇²φ − Σ_a φ + S = 0  (steady state)

where D = diffusion coefficient (~1 cm for water), Σ_a = macroscopic absorption cross-section, S = source.

For a critical reactor S = ν Σ_f φ (each fission produces ν new neutrons). Substituting:
  D ∇²φ + (ν Σ_f − Σ_a) φ = 0
  ∇²φ + B² φ = 0

where **B² = (ν Σ_f − Σ_a)/D** is the **material buckling**.

For a bare cylindrical core of radius R + height H:
  ∇²φ = (1/r)d(r dφ/dr)/dr + d²φ/dz²

Separation of variables gives Bessel + cosine solutions:
  φ(r,z) = φ_0 J_0(2.405 r/R̃) cos(πz/H̃)

with **geometric buckling** B_g² = (2.405/R̃)² + (π/H̃)². For criticality: material buckling = geometric buckling (B_m² = B_g²).

**Critical size**: solve for the smallest dimensions that satisfy the criticality condition. Reflected reactors have effective dimensions R̃ = R + 2δ (extrapolation distance) — reflector pushes critical radius smaller.

Modern reactor design uses **multi-group diffusion** (separating energy groups) + **transport codes** (MCNP, OpenMC for Monte Carlo; ATTILA, PARTISN for deterministic). 3D-coupled neutronics + thermal-hydraulics (CASMO, SIMULATE, MPACT, BISON) for full core analysis.

slides.title: Reactivity, control, + feedback
slides.body:
**Reactivity**: ρ = (k_eff − 1) / k_eff. Units:
• **pcm**: per-cent-mille = 10⁻⁵ (most common)
• **$**: ρ/β where β is delayed neutron fraction
• Negative ρ = subcritical; positive = supercritical.

**Reactivity sources**:
• **Control rods**: insert into core; absorb neutrons; reduce f → reduce k. Worth: ~5-20 $ for a bank.
• **Soluble boron** (PWRs): boric acid in coolant; absorbs neutrons. Gradually reduced as fuel depletes.
• **Burnable poisons** (Gd in fuel, Er): high initial absorption that depletes with fuel → balances reactivity.
• **Fuel composition**: as U-235 + Pu-239 deplete + fission products accumulate, k_∞ drops.
• **Temperature**: Doppler broadening (fuel T ↑ → U-238 resonance absorption ↑ → k ↓; **negative coefficient**, ~−3 pcm/°C). Moderator T (water): density ↓ → moderation ↓ → k ↓ (mostly negative in PWRs; positive in some void-coefficient designs like the RBMK Chernobyl reactor).
• **Xenon poisoning**: Xe-135 has σ_a = 2.6×10⁶ barns — massive thermal absorber. Builds up after shutdown from I-135 → Xe-135 chain (peak ~12 hr post-shutdown). Can prevent restart for 24-48 hr — 'xenon precluded' state.

**Reactor period** T = ln(2) × t_double = (β − ρ)/(λ ρ) (for ρ > 0, ρ < β). Long period = safe. Short period = approaching prompt critical.

**Prompt critical** = when ρ ≥ β (= 1$): delayed neutrons no longer control kinetics; chain reaction races on Λ ~ 10⁻⁴ s timescale. Power doubles in milliseconds. Chernobyl 1986: reactivity excursion crossed 1$ → power surge → steam explosion. Modern designs make this impossible by inherent reactivity limits.

question.question: Compute k_∞ for an LWR fuel + estimate control-rod worth
question.goal: PWR with η = 2.07, f = 0.71, p = 0.79, ε = 1.04. Compute k_∞, then calculate how much reduction in f (e.g., by control rod insertion) brings k_∞ down to 1.0.

steps.reveal: ρ = 0.207/1.207 ≈ 17.2% ≈ 17,200 pcm. Must be controlled by poison + rods + leakage.

steps.prompt: If we reduce f from 0.71 to 0.59 (control rod insertion), what's k_∞?
steps.reveal: k_∞ = 2.07 × 0.59 × 0.79 × 1.04 ≈ 1.00. So reducing f by ~17% brings reactor critical.

steps.prompt: Δf = 0.12. What's the reactivity worth of this rod insertion?
steps.reveal: ρ_worth ≈ 17% ≈ 17,000 pcm ≈ 26$. A large rod bank. Real PWRs have multiple banks worth different amounts; total worth designed for shutdown margin + safety + cold-shutdown capability.

question.question: Why is xenon-135 a special concern for reactor operators despite being just one isotope?
options: Xe-135 has σ_a = 2.6×10⁶ barns — the largest thermal-neutron cross-section of any nuclide. Even small amounts (parts per trillion of fuel) absorb significant neutrons. Builds up from I-135 decay after shutdown; peaks ~12 hr later; can preclude restart for 24-48 hr. Equilibrium during operation costs ~3% reactivity. Mismanagement contributed to Chernobyl 1986 — operators in xenon-dip tried to maintain power with excessive control rod withdrawal, leading to positive-void-coefficient runaway.
question.explanation:
Xe-135 cross-section (2.6×10⁶ barns) is ~5000× larger than U-235 fission. Even tiny amounts dominate neutron absorption.

**Production chain**: fission → Te-135 → I-135 (t₁/₂ = 6.7 hr) → Xe-135 (t₁/₂ = 9.2 hr).

**During operation**: Xe-135 produced by fission + I-135 decay; destroyed by neutron absorption + decay. Steady-state equilibrium loses ~3% reactivity.

**After shutdown**: production from I-135 decay continues; destruction by absorption stops. Xe-135 inventory peaks 10-12 hr post-shutdown — 'xenon peak' — adding ~10-30% negative reactivity. Restart impossible until xenon decays (24-48 hr) or via reactor reactivity reserve.

**Xenon oscillations**: in large cores, xenon distribution can become unstable, with oscillating high/low concentrations across the core. Modern operations + control monitor this.

**Chernobyl 1986**: experiment paused mid-operation; xenon built up; operators withdrew control rods to compensate; reactor in marginally-stable + reactivity-vulnerable state. Coolant flow disturbance + positive void coefficient → power surge → prompt critical → steam explosion + graphite fire. Soviet RBMK design had unique vulnerabilities (positive void at low power, graphite tip on control rods causing initial reactivity insertion).

Xenon management is part of every operator's training — limit rates of power change, observe xenon peak, plan shutdowns + restarts around xenon dynamics.

slides.workedSolution: Xe-135 σ_a = 2.6×10⁶ barns — largest of any nuclide. Production: I-135 decay (after fission). Destruction: neutron absorption + decay. Equilibrium during operation costs ~3% reactivity. Post-shutdown: production continues, destruction stops → peak 10-12 hr later, +10-30% negative reactivity. Can preclude restart 24-48 hr. Chernobyl 1986: xenon mismanagement + RBMK positive void → runaway.

question.question: Why do LWRs use water as a moderator + light-water reactors dominate globally?
options: Water moderates fast neutrons to thermal in ~25 collisions (vs ~2000 for U), enabling small core size; provides excellent heat transfer; readily available + cheap; well-characterized chemistry. Trade-off: water absorbs neutrons (Σ_a ~ 0.022 cm⁻¹), so LWRs need enriched fuel (3-5% U-235) vs natural-uranium reactors (CANDU heavy-water). LWRs dominate because of operating economics + military heritage (US Navy submarine fleet drove development).
All other materials are too expensive.
question.explanation:
**Moderator comparison**: H₂O, D₂O (heavy water), graphite, beryllium are the practical choices. Key metrics:

• **Moderating ratio** ξ Σ_s / Σ_a — slowing-down power per absorption:
  - H₂O: ~58 (good slowing, modest absorption)
  - D₂O: ~9000 (excellent slowing, very low absorption)
  - Graphite: ~190
  - Beryllium: ~150

• **Slowing-down length** (slows fast → thermal in <Δr²>^(1/2) cm):
  - H₂O: ~6 cm
  - D₂O: ~11 cm
  - Graphite: ~19 cm

Water absorbs more neutrons but slows much faster + is much denser. So LWRs are compact (~3 m core dia) but need enriched fuel. CANDU (heavy water) can use natural U but needs larger core (~7 m). RBMK + Magnox: graphite-moderated, large cores, natural U.

**Economic + historical drivers**:
1. Westinghouse + GE developed PWR + BWR for US Navy submarines (Rickover 1950s) — small, high-power-density, water-cooled.
2. Civilian LWR designs (Shippingport 1957, Yankee Rowe 1961) followed.
3. Enrichment infrastructure became cheap (gaseous diffusion, then centrifuge).
4. Reliability + operational experience accumulated.
5. By 1970s-80s, LWR dominated global commercial market.

**~80% of current commercial reactors are LWRs (PWR + BWR)**. CANDU: ~10%. Graphite-moderated: ~5% (remaining UK Magnox + Russia RBMK). Fast reactors: a few demonstration units.

LWR's economic + operational maturity is hard to dislodge. SMR designs (NuScale, BWRX-300) are largely LWR variants. Some Gen IV designs (Molten Salt, sodium-cooled, gas-cooled) target niches but won't displace LWRs at scale soon.

hints: What's special about water as moderator?
slides.workedSolution: Water moderates fast neutrons in ~25 collisions (vs ~2000 for U), provides excellent heat transfer, cheap, well-characterized. Trade-off: absorbs neutrons so needs 3-5% enriched fuel. Heavy water absorbs less so CANDU uses natural U (cheaper fuel) but larger core. LWR dominance: Navy heritage (Rickover), enrichment infrastructure scaled, operational experience. ~80% of commercial reactors LWR globally. SMRs largely LWR variants.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why the 'four-factor formula' is both pedagogically useful + practically limited.
question.rubric: Mentions: k_∞ = η·f·p·ε decomposes neutron balance into intuitive physical mechanisms. Each factor maps to a design choice: η to fuel; f to fuel-moderator ratio; p to fuel lump size + moderator spacing; ε to fast spectrum contribution. Useful for back-of-envelope design + operator intuition. Limits: assumes infinite homogeneous medium; ignores leakage (finite-size effect); spatial + energy variations of flux not captured; depletion + isotopic build-up not directly handled; non-uniform fuel loading + control patterns ignored. Real design uses multi-group diffusion + transport codes (MCNP, OpenMC, CASMO+SIMULATE, MPACT) that solve full Boltzmann transport. Four-factor remains a conceptual scaffold + sanity check on advanced calculations.
